name: Điện Biên Phủ Battlefield
localName: Di tích Chiến trường Điện Biên Phủ
summary: The valley where Vietnamese forces besieged and defeated the French army in 1954, ending French rule in Indochina. Hills, bunkers and a museum keep the story.

hero.file: Victory in Battle of Dien Bien Phu.jpg
hero.alt: Soldiers raise the flag over the French command bunker in 1954

eras.label: Nov 1953
eras.title: Paratroopers in the valley
eras.text: In November 1953, French paratroopers landed in the remote valley. They built a fortified camp with an airstrip and strongpoints on the surrounding hills, hoping to draw the Việt Minh into a pitched battle.

image.file: French M24s atr Dien Bien Phu.jpg
image.alt: French tanks at Điện Biên Phủ

eras.label: March 1954
eras.title: The siege begins
eras.text: On 13 March 1954, Vietnamese artillery, hauled over the mountains by hand, opened fire on the strongpoint of Him Lam. Tens of thousands of porters carried food and ammunition to the front on foot and by bicycle.

image.file: Dân công dân tộc vận chuyển hàng ra mặt trận.jpg
image.alt: Porters carrying supplies to the front

eras.label: 7 May 1954
eras.title: Victory
eras.text: After 56 days of fighting, Vietnamese soldiers reached the command bunker of General de Castries on 7 May and raised their flag. The French garrison surrendered, and the peace talks in Geneva soon ended the war.

image.file: Victory in Battle of Dien Bien Phu.jpg
image.alt: Raising the flag over the command bunker

eras.title: A new museum
eras.text: For the 60th anniversary, a new museum opened at the foot of A1 Hill, with weapons, maps and the stories of soldiers and porters.

image.file: Captured French artillery at the Dien Bien Phu Museum.jpg
image.alt: Captured French artillery at the museum

eras.label: Today
eras.title: The Victory Monument
eras.text: A bronze monument on D1 Hill, raised in 2004, looks out over the valley. Visitors walk the trenches of A1 Hill and step down into the restored command bunker.

image.file: The Victory Monument of Dien Bien Phu (front).jpg
image.alt: The Điện Biên Phủ Victory Monument

story.title: Guns over the mountains

image.file: Phao phong khong To Vinh Dien.JPG
image.alt: An anti-aircraft gun at Điện Biên Phủ

story.narration: The French believed no one could bring heavy artillery through the jungle and over the mountains around the valley. The Vietnamese did it by hand. Teams of soldiers hauled guns up steep slopes with ropes, a few hundred metres a night. A story told in every Vietnamese school is about Tô Vĩnh Diện, a soldier who, when a rope snapped, threw himself under the wheel of a gun to stop it rolling down the slope. When the bombardment began on 13 March, the guns were firing from hidden positions high above the French camp.

story.title: The bicycles that carried a war

image.file: Dân công dân tộc vận chuyển hàng ra mặt trận.jpg

story.narration: Behind the soldiers came an army of porters, many of them farmers and young women from the delta and the mountains. They carried rice, ammunition and medicine for hundreds of kilometres along jungle tracks, mostly at night to avoid French aircraft. Many pushed bicycles strengthened with bamboo and wood. Loaded with more than 200 kilograms each, the bicycles were steered by a pole tied to the handlebars. Supplying the siege was as much a victory as the fighting itself.

story.title: 7 May 1954
story.narration: By early May, the French held only a small area around their command post. On the afternoon of 7 May, Vietnamese soldiers reached the bunker of General Christian de Castries and raised a flag over it. That evening the firing stopped. More than ten thousand French and colonial soldiers were taken prisoner. The next day, peace talks on Indochina began in Geneva. Today you can climb down into a reconstruction of the bunker, and walk the trenches of A1 Hill, where some of the hardest fighting took place.

guide.price: Small separate tickets for the museum, A1 Hill, the de Castries bunker and Him Lam Hill.

hours.notes: Approximate. Each site has its own gate and ticket.

do: Start at the museum to understand the layout of the battle.
Walk the trenches on A1 Hill, and climb D1 Hill for the view over the valley.
Visit the war cemetery opposite A1 Hill.
dont: Climb on weapons or vehicles on display.
Make jokes or pose playfully at the cemetery.
Wander off marked paths on the hills.

tips.title: Thái food
tips.text: Try grilled fish (pa pỉnh tộp), sticky rice and Điện Biên rice, considered among the best in the north.

tips.title: Getting there
tips.text: Flights from Hà Nội take about an hour; the bus takes 10–12 hours over the Pha Đin Pass.

tips.title: In season
tips.text: In March the hills around the valley are white with ban flowers.
